title: Sunburn & Sun Poisoning in Cabo: Relief and When to Call
description: Bad sunburn or sun poisoning in Cabo? What helps, warning signs that need a doctor, and how to get a house call ($199) or IV hydration at your hotel 24/7.

intro: The sun in Los Cabos is strong all year, and many visitors underestimate it on the first day — a long boat tour, a nap by the pool or an afternoon on the beach can be enough for a painful burn. Most sunburns heal on their own with simple care, but a severe burn with blisters, fever or vomiting, often called sun poisoning, can make you feel genuinely ill.
This guide explains what usually helps, the warning signs that mean you should see a doctor, and how to get care at your hotel, villa or yacht without spending a vacation day in a waiting room.

sections.h2: Sunburn vs. sun poisoning: what's the difference?
p: A regular sunburn makes the skin red, warm, tender and sometimes itchy for a few days before it peels. "Sun poisoning" is not a medical diagnosis but a common name for a severe sunburn that affects your whole body. It may come with:
list: Large areas of blistering skin
Fever, chills or shaking
Headache, nausea or vomiting
Dizziness, weakness or feeling faint
Swelling of the burned skin, especially legs and feet
An itchy, bumpy rash on sun-exposed skin
p_after: Symptoms often build during the first day after sun exposure. Because a bad burn also pulls fluid toward the skin, many travelers with sun poisoning are dehydrated at the same time — especially after drinking alcohol in the heat.

sections.h2: What usually helps at your hotel
p: For a mild to moderate sunburn, these general steps help most people feel better:
list: Get out of the sun completely and stay in the shade or indoors until the skin calms down.
Cool the skin with cool (not ice-cold) showers or damp cloths. Do not put ice directly on burned skin.
Moisturize gently with aloe vera gel or a fragrance-free moisturizer. Pharmacies in Cabo sell both.
Drink more fluids than usual — water and oral rehydration salts — and go easy on alcohol until you recover.
Leave blisters alone. Popping them raises the risk of infection; cover broken blisters loosely with a clean bandage.
Wear loose, soft clothing made of cotton, and avoid tight straps over burned areas.
Ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking any pain reliever, especially if you take other medication, are pregnant, or are treating a child.
p_after: Avoid home remedies like butter, oils, petroleum jelly or numbing sprays on badly burned skin — they can trap heat or irritate the skin further.

p: Call a doctor the same day if you or someone in your group has:
list: Blisters covering a large area (for example, most of the back or both legs)
Fever above 102°F (38.9°C), chills or vomiting
Signs of dehydration: very little urine, dry mouth, dizziness or a racing heart
Severe pain that keeps you from sleeping or moving normally
Signs of infection: increasing redness, warmth, pus or red streaks spreading from a blister
A sunburned baby or young child, an older adult, a pregnant traveler or someone with a chronic illness
A rash or burn after taking a new medication, since some medicines make skin more sensitive to the sun
p_after: Call 911 right away for confusion, fainting, seizures, a very high body temperature with hot skin, trouble breathing, or a person who stops sweating and seems disoriented in the heat. These can be signs of heat stroke, which is a medical emergency.

sections.h2: Getting care without leaving your room

p: An English-speaking doctor comes to your hotel, villa or yacht 24/7, examines the burn, checks for dehydration and infection, and prescribes medication if appropriate. Typical arrival is 30–45 minutes in Cabo San Lucas and the Tourist Corridor, and up to about 60 minutes in San José del Cabo, Pedregal and Palmilla. Clinic consultations are $99. sections.h2: Sun safety tips for the rest of your trip
list: Use a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen and reapply often, especially after swimming or sweating.
Plan beach time and boat tours for the morning or late afternoon, and seek shade around midday.
Wear a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses and a long-sleeve rash guard on the water — sun reflects off the ocean and sand.
Remember that clouds and breezes do not block UV rays; you can burn on a cool, windy day.
Keep drinking water throughout the day, and alternate alcoholic drinks with water.
Check the label of any medication you take: some antibiotics and other medicines increase sun sensitivity.

sections.h2: Sunburn and alcohol: a tough combination
p: A day of sun, cocktails and little water is one of the most common reasons travelers feel awful the next morning. Alcohol adds to fluid loss, and a sunburn makes it harder to notice early dehydration. If you wake up with a burn, a headache and nausea, rest in the shade, sip fluids slowly and call a doctor if you cannot keep them down. Our guide to what to do if you get sick in Cabo covers more common vacation illnesses.

faq.q: How long does sun poisoning last?
faq.a: Many people start feeling better within a few days, while peeling can continue for about a week. If you have fever, vomiting, large blisters or signs of dehydration, see a doctor rather than waiting it out.

faq.q: Can I get an IV for sunburn or sun poisoning in Cabo?
faq.a: An IV does not heal the burn itself, but if you are dehydrated from too much sun, a licensed nurse can give you IV fluids at your hotel or villa. IV drips start at $159 plus tax at your door, or $129 plus tax at our clinic.
No. Leave blisters intact to lower the risk of infection. If one breaks, keep it clean and loosely covered, and see a doctor if it becomes more red, warm or painful.

faq.q: How much does a doctor visit for a sunburn cost in Cabo?
faq.a: A house call to your hotel, villa or yacht is $199 USD, and a clinic consultation is $99 USD. You pay after the visit and get an itemized invoice for travel insurance.

faq.q: When is a sunburn an emergency?
faq.a: Call 911 for confusion, fainting, seizures, trouble breathing, or a very high temperature with hot skin. These can be signs of heat stroke.
